## Where we got to last class
### Web APIs without writing code

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- An [API]{.alert} is a contract: ask this way, get that back
- A URL has a host, a [path]{.alert} (what you want), and a [query string]{.alert} (how you want it)
- A [status code]{.alert} says how it went: `2xx` worked, `4xx` is your mistake, `5xx` is theirs
- The World Bank answers some errors with `200`, so look at the data too
- [JSON]{.alert} is made of objects `{ }` and arrays `[ ]`
- A value is reached by a [path]{.alert}, such as `current` → `temperature_2m`
- `curl -o` saved a reply to a file
- Four lines of Python did the same as `curl`
::::

# Reading JSON in Python 🐍 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Dictionaries and lists
### The two Python types that hold JSON

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
```python
course = {"code": "DATASCI 350", "enrolled": 40,
          "instructor": {"name": "Danilo Freire"}}
years = [2023, 2024, 2025]

print(course["code"])
print(course["instructor"]["name"])
print(years[0], years[2])
print(type(course), type(years))
```

```text
DATASCI 350
Danilo Freire
2023 2025
<class 'dict'> <class 'list'>
```
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- A [dictionary]{.alert} (`dict`) is Python's JSON object: `{"key": value}`
- You get a value by its key: `course["code"]`
- A [list]{.alert} is Python's JSON array: `[a, b, c]`
- You get a value by its position, from 0: `years[0]`
- A dictionary can hold another dictionary. Each step of the path adds one pair of brackets
- `course["instructor"]["name"]` is the path `instructor` → `name` from last class
::::
:::
:::

## Opening a file
### What `with open(...) as f:` means

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
```python
import json

with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json") as f:
    wb = json.load(f)

print(type(wb))
print(len(wb))
```

```text
<class 'list'>
2
```

:::{style="font-size: 18px;"}
The file is last class's `curl -o` download: [`wb_gdp_bra.json`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-19/data/wb_gdp_bra.json). Save it in a `data/` folder next to your notebook
:::
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- `open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json")` finds the file and prepares it for reading
- `as f` gives the [open file]{.alert} a short name, `f`
- The indented lines run while the file is open
- When they finish, Python [closes the file]{.alert} for you
- `json.load(f)` reads the JSON text and turns it into Python objects
- The World Bank reply is a list of two items, as we saw last class
::::
:::
:::

## `json.load` and `json.loads`
### One reads a file, the other reads a string

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
import json

text = '{"city": "Atlanta", "temperature": 29.6, "raining": false}'
data = json.loads(text)

print(type(text))
print(type(data))
print(data["city"], data["raining"])
```

```text
<class 'str'>
<class 'dict'>
Atlanta False
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- [`json.load(f)`]{.alert} reads JSON from an open file
- [`json.loads(text)`]{.alert} reads JSON from a string. The `s` stands for "string"
- Before: one long piece of text. After: a dictionary you can index
- JSON `false` became Python `False`
- Later today, `r.json()` does the same for an API reply
::::
:::
:::

## From a path to square brackets
### The World Bank reply, one step per line

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
```python
import json

with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json") as f:
    wb = json.load(f)

meta = wb[0]
records = wb[1]
first = records[0]

print(meta["total"])
print(first["date"], first["value"])
print(first["country"]["value"])
```

```text
12
2025 9747.99557762692
Brazil
```
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- `wb[0]` is the metadata, and `wb[1]` is the list of records
- Giving each step a name, like `meta` and `records`, makes the code easy to read
- `records[0]` is the newest year, 2025
- `first["country"]["value"]` is the path `country` → `value`
- You could write `wb[1][0]["country"]["value"]` in one go. It is the same path
::::
:::
:::

## When a path is wrong
### Two errors you will see, and what to do about them

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
```python
first["year"]
```

```text
KeyError: 'year'
```

- A [`KeyError`]{.alert} means the dictionary has no such key
- Here the key is called `date`, not `year`

```python
wb[2]
```

```text
IndexError: list index out of range
```

- An [`IndexError`]{.alert} means the list is shorter than you think
- `wb` has two items, at positions 0 and 1
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- When a path fails, [print the step before it]{.alert}
- `.keys()` lists the keys of a dictionary
- `len()` gives the length of a list

```python
print(first.keys())
```

```text
dict_keys(['indicator', 'country',
'countryiso3code', 'date', 'value',
'unit', 'obs_status', 'decimal'])
```

- Now you can see the right name, and fix the path
::::
:::
:::

# `requests`, step by step 🌐 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What comes back from `requests.get`
### A response object, with the reply inside

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
```python
import requests

url = "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m"
r = requests.get(url, timeout=30)

print(type(r))
print(r.status_code)
print(r.text[:60])

data = r.json()
print(type(data))
```

```text
<class 'requests.models.Response'>
200
{"latitude":33.759865,"longitude":-84.39586,"generationtime_
<class 'dict'>
```

- `requests.get` returns a [response]{.alert}, which we call `r`
- `r.status_code` is the status code
- `r.text` is the reply as plain text. `[:60]` shows the first 60 characters
- `r.json()` turns that text into a dictionary, like `json.loads`
- [`timeout=30`]{.alert} gives up after 30 seconds. Without it, a silent server can make your script wait forever
- Install `requests` once with `pip install requests`
:::

## Let `requests` build the URL
### Put the options in a dictionary called `params`

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
```python
import requests

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
params = {
    "format": "json",
    "date": "2014:2025",
}

r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
print(r.url)
print(r.status_code)
```

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json&date=2014%3A2025
200
```

- The `url` holds only the path. No `?` and no `&`
- Each key in `params` becomes one option in the query string
- `requests` adds the `?` and the `&` for you
- It also percent-encodes the values: `:` became `%3A`
- `r.url` shows the full URL that was sent. Paste it into your browser to check it
- To change the years, you change one value, not a long string
:::

## Checking for errors
### `raise_for_status()` stops the script on a bad status

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
A typo in the path: `countryy` instead of `country`

```python
url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/countryy/BRA"
r = requests.get(url, params={"format": "json"}, timeout=30)
print(r.status_code)
r.raise_for_status()
```

```text
404
requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error:
Not Found for url: https://api.worldbank.org/v2/
countryy/BRA?format=json
```

- `r.raise_for_status()` checks the status code
- If it is `4xx` or `5xx`, it [raises an error]{.alert}: Python stops and prints a message
- If the status is `2xx`, it does nothing and the script carries on
- Stopping early is good. You see the problem where it happens, not ten lines later
- Put it right after every `requests.get`
:::

## The World Bank's hidden error
### A `200` that carries an error message

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
A country code that does not exist, `XYZ`:

```python
url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/XYZ/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
r = requests.get(url, params={"format": "json"}, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
payload = r.json()

print(r.status_code)
print(len(payload))
if len(payload) < 2:
    print("No data:", payload[0]["message"][0]["value"])
```

```text
200
1
No data: The provided parameter value is not valid
```

- The status is `200`, so `raise_for_status()` lets it pass
- A good World Bank reply has [two]{.alert} items: metadata and data
- This one has only one, holding an error message
- `if len(payload) < 2:` catches it
- The status tells you the request arrived. [The data tells you whether it worked]{.alert}
:::

## A complete request
### Ask, check, and save

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
```python
import json
import requests

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
params = {"format": "json", "date": "2014:2025"}

r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
payload = r.json()

if len(payload) < 2:
    print("No data:", payload)
else:
    with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)
    print("Saved", payload[0]["total"], "records")
```

```text
Saved 12 records
```

- This is the Python version of last class's `curl -o`
- `open(..., "w")` opens the file for [writing]{.alert}. It creates the file, or replaces it
- `json.dump` is the reverse of `json.load`: it turns Python objects into JSON text in a file
- `indent=2` makes the file readable, like `json.tool`
- The `else:` block runs only when the check passes, so a bad reply is never saved
:::

# From JSON to a DataFrame 🐼 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## A loop that picks the fields
### One small dictionary per record

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
records = wb[1]

rows = []
for record in records:
    row = {
        "country": record["country"]["value"],
        "year": int(record["date"]),
        "value": record["value"],
    }
    rows.append(row)

print(len(rows))
print(rows[0])
```

```text
12
{'country': 'Brazil', 'year': 2025, 'value': 9747.99557762692}
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- Each World Bank record has eight fields, some nested. We want three
- `rows = []` starts an empty list
- `for record in records:` runs the indented lines once per record
- Each time, we build a small dictionary with the [three fields we want]{.alert}
- `rows.append(row)` adds it to the end of the list
- `int(record["date"])` turns the year from text, `"2025"`, into a number, `2025`
::::
:::
:::

## From a list of dictionaries to a DataFrame
### Each dictionary becomes a row

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df = df.sort_values("year")
df = df.reset_index(drop=True)

print(df.head())
print(df.shape)
```

```text
  country  year        value
0  Brazil  2014  9338.342783
1  Brazil  2015  8936.196617
2  Brazil  2016  8577.843767
3  Brazil  2017  8628.253089
4  Brazil  2018  8722.336303
(12, 3)
```
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- `pd.DataFrame(rows)` makes one row per dictionary
- The keys, `country`, `year` and `value`, become the column names
- `sort_values("year")` puts the oldest year first
- `reset_index(drop=True)` renumbers the rows from 0 after sorting
- `df.shape` is (rows, columns): 12 years, 3 columns
- From here on, it is ordinary pandas
::::
:::
:::

## A shortcut: `pd.json_normalize`
### It flattens every field for you

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
flat = pd.json_normalize(records)
print(flat.columns.tolist())

df = flat[["country.value", "date", "value"]]
print(df.head(3))
```

```text
['countryiso3code', 'date', 'value', 'unit',
 'obs_status', 'decimal', 'indicator.id',
 'indicator.value', 'country.id', 'country.value']

  country.value  date        value
0        Brazil  2025  9747.995578
1        Brazil  2024  9566.745187
2        Brazil  2023  9288.027015
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `json_normalize` keeps [all]{.alert} the fields, ten columns here
- A nested field gets a name with a dot: `country` → `value` becomes `country.value`
- You then choose the columns you want with double brackets
- `date` is still text here. The loop turned it into a number
- Both ways work. The loop is longer, but you see every step
::::
:::
:::

## Many countries in one request
### Join the country codes with `;`

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
Life expectancy for five countries, 2000 to 2024

```python
url = ("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/"
       "BRA;IND;JPN;NGA;USA/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN")
params = {"format": "json", "date": "2000:2024",
          "per_page": 1000}
```

Then the same loop and `pd.DataFrame(rows)`:

```python
print(df.shape)
print(df["country"].value_counts())
```

```text
(125, 3)
country
Brazil           25
India            25
Japan            25
Nigeria          25
United States    25
Name: count, dtype: int64
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `BRA;IND;JPN;NGA;USA` asks for five countries at once
- `SP.DYN.LE00.IN` is life expectancy at birth
- 5 countries × 25 years = [125 records]{.alert}
- The World Bank sends 50 records per page by default
- `per_page=1000` gets them all in one reply, so there is only one page to read
- Saved reply: [`wb_life_expectancy_5.json`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-19/data/wb_life_expectancy_5.json)
::::
:::
:::

## Missing values
### Some years have no data yet

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
The same loop, with `BRA;NGA` and the years `2022:2025`

```python
print(df)
```

```text
   country  year   value
0   Brazil  2025     NaN
1   Brazil  2024  76.023
2   Brazil  2023  75.848
3   Brazil  2022  74.872
4  Nigeria  2025     NaN
5  Nigeria  2024  54.635
6  Nigeria  2023  54.462
7  Nigeria  2022  54.079
```

```python
df = df.dropna()
print(len(df))
```

```text
6
```
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- The World Bank has not published 2025 life expectancy yet
- It sends those years with `"value": null`
- JSON `null` becomes Python `None`, and pandas shows it as [`NaN`]{.alert} ("not a number")
- `dropna()` removes the rows with missing values
- A missing value is [not a zero]{.alert}. Say in your report how you handled it
::::
:::
:::

## A first analysis, and saving the table
### Back to the five-country table

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
latest = df[df["year"] == 2024]
latest = latest.sort_values("value", ascending=False)
print(latest)

df.to_csv("data/life_expectancy.csv", index=False)
```

```text
           country  year      value
50           Japan  2024  84.036341
100  United States  2024  78.890244
0           Brazil  2024  76.023000
25           India  2024  72.235000
75         Nigeria  2024  54.635000
```

The CSV starts like this:

```text
country,year,value
Brazil,2024,76.023
Brazil,2023,75.848
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `df[df["year"] == 2024]` keeps only the rows for 2024
- `ascending=False` puts the highest value first
- The numbers on the left are the original row labels
- `to_csv` writes the table to a file your report can read
- `index=False` leaves out those row labels, which are not data
- Parquet is a smaller, faster format. Lecture 21 covers it
::::
:::
:::

# Your project's pull script 🗺️ {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Today's lecture is your project's first step
### Four stages, and you now have the first two

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-bottom: 20px;"}
[![](figures/project-pipeline-diagram.png){width="85%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/project-pipeline-diagram.png"}
:::

- [Collect]{.alert}: `requests` pulls data from a web API, as we did today
- [Snapshot]{.alert}: the script saves the raw reply and a tidy CSV in `data/raw/`
- [Analyse]{.alert}: pandas or DuckDB do the work, and Quarto writes the report
- [Ship]{.alert}: a Docker container renders the report on anyone's machine, later in the course
:::

## `pull_data.py`, part 1: the settings
### The only lines you have to change

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
# The World Bank indicator code. This one is
# life expectancy at birth.
INDICATOR = "SP.DYN.LE00.IN"

# The countries you want, as ISO three-letter
# codes, joined by ";".
COUNTRIES = "BRA;IND;NGA;USA"

# The years to cover, written as "first:last".
YEARS = "2000:2023"

# A short, readable name for the output files.
OUTPUT_NAME = "life_expectancy"
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- The script is in the [starter repository](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350-project-starter), under `scripts/`
- These four settings sit at the top of the file
- Names in capital letters are [constants]{.alert}: values that stay the same while the script runs
- `COUNTRIES` uses the `;` you saw today
- Pick your indicators at [data.worldbank.org/indicator](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator)
- Everything below the settings rarely needs changing
::::
:::
:::

## `pull_data.py`, part 2: the request
### Everything from the `requests` section, in one function

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="57%"}
```python
def fetch_indicator(indicator, countries, years):
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/country/{countries}/indicator/{indicator}"
    params = {
        "format": "json",
        "date": years,
        "per_page": 20000,
    }
    response = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=60)
    response.raise_for_status()

    payload = response.json()
    if not isinstance(payload, list) or len(payload) < 2:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected response from the API: {payload}")

    return payload
```

:::{style="font-size: 17px;"}
Comments and type hints removed to fit the slide. The file itself explains every line
:::
::::

::::{.column width="43%"}
- `def` creates a [function]{.alert}: a named block of code you can run later
- `return payload` hands the reply back to whoever called the function
- The `f"..."` string fills in the values inside `{ }`. `BASE_URL` is set near the top of the file: `https://api.worldbank.org/v2`
- `per_page=20000` fits everything on one page
- `raise RuntimeError(...)` stops the script with a message, like `raise_for_status()`
- The length check is the one we wrote today
::::
:::
:::

## `pull_data.py`, part 3: the table
### Today's loop, written in a shorter form

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}

The starter's version

```python
rows = [
    {
        "country_code": record["countryiso3code"],
        "country": record["country"]["value"],
        "indicator": record["indicator"]["id"],
        "year": int(record["date"]),
        "value": record["value"],
    }
    for record in records
]
frame = pd.DataFrame(rows)
frame = frame.dropna(subset=["value"])
```
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
Today's version, which does the same

```python
rows = []
for record in records:
    rows.append({
        "country_code": record["countryiso3code"],
        "country": record["country"]["value"],
        "indicator": record["indicator"]["id"],
        "year": int(record["date"]),
        "value": record["value"],
    })
```

- The starter uses a [list comprehension]{.alert}: the `for` goes inside the brackets

## If your API needs a key or sends pages
### Only for Track B. The World Bank needs neither

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
#### API keys

- Some APIs need a key, a password for programs
- You used one in Lecture 14
- Keep it in a [`.env` file]{.alert}, and put `.env` in `.gitignore`
- [Never commit a key.]{.alert} Bots find them in public repositories within minutes
- Details and code: [Appendix 04](#sec:appendix04)
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
#### Pages

- Some APIs send long results in [pages]{.alert}
- The reply says how many pages there are
- You ask for page 1, then page 2, and so on, until the last one
- First try a bigger page, like `per_page=20000`. One request is simpler than a loop
- Details and code: [Appendix 05](#sec:appendix05)
::::
:::
:::

# Conclusion 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What we learned today
### From an API reply to a saved table, in Python

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- JSON objects become [dictionaries]{.alert}, and arrays become [lists]{.alert}
- `with open(...) as f:` opens a file and closes it for you
- `json.load` reads JSON, and `json.dump` writes it
- A path becomes square brackets: `wb[1][0]["value"]`
- `requests.get(url, params=..., timeout=30)` sends the request
- `raise_for_status()` and a length check catch the errors
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- A `for` loop picks the fields you want from each record
- `pd.DataFrame(rows)` turns the list into a table
- `;` asks for many countries, and `per_page` gets them in one reply
- `null` becomes `NaN`, and `dropna()` removes it
- `to_csv(..., index=False)` saves the table for your report
- Your project's `pull_data.py` does all of this, and you can now read every line
::::
:::

## Appendix 01 {#sec:appendix01}
### Exercise 01 solution

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
```python
import json

with open("data/wb_pop_ury.json") as f:
    wb = json.load(f)

print(wb[0]["total"])
print(wb[1][5]["date"], wb[1][5]["value"])
print(wb[1][0]["country"]["value"])
```

```text
12
2020 3398968
Uruguay
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `wb[0]` is the metadata, and `total` is one of its keys
- Records run newest first, so 2020 is at position `5` (2025 is at `0`)
- Last class's path `1` → `5` → `value` becomes `wb[1][5]["value"]`
- Every record holds the country, so `wb[1][0]` works as well as any other

## Appendix 02 {#sec:appendix02}
### Exercise 02 solution

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="57%"}
```python
import json
import requests

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/URY/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL"
params = {"format": "json", "date": "2014:2025"}

r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
payload = r.json()

if len(payload) < 2:
    print("No data:", payload)
else:
    with open("data/wb_pop_ury.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)
    print(r.url)
    print("Saved", payload[0]["total"], "records")
```

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/URY/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json&date=2014%3A2025
Saved 12 records
```
::::

::::{.column width="43%"}
- Only `URY` and `SP.POP.TOTL` changed. The `params` are the same for every indicator
- With `XYZ`, the length check prints the "No data" message, and no file is written
- If the `data/` folder does not exist, `open` fails. Create the folder first

```python
import requests
import pandas as pd

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/ARG;BRA;URY/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
params = {"format": "json", "date": "2014:2025", "per_page": 1000}

r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
payload = r.json()

rows = []
for record in payload[1]:
    rows.append({
        "country": record["country"]["value"],
        "year": int(record["date"]),
        "value": record["value"],
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.shape)
print(df["value"].isna().sum())

latest = df[df["year"] == 2025]
latest = latest.sort_values("value", ascending=False)
print(latest)

df.to_csv("data/gdp_south_america.csv", index=False)
```

## Appendix 04: API keys {#sec:appendix04}
### For Track B APIs that ask who you are

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
1. Sign up on the API's website. The key usually arrives by email in a minute
2. Put it in a file called [`.env`]{.alert}, one `NAME=value` per line, with no quotes

```
NASA_API_KEY=abc123def456
```

3. Add `.env` to your [`.gitignore`]{.alert} [before]{.alert} your first commit
4. Read it in Python with `python-dotenv`, as in Lecture 14

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
key = os.getenv("NASA_API_KEY")
```
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
5. Send it the way the documentation says:

```python
# In the query string
params = {"api_key": key}

# Or in a header, which is safer
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}
r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30)
```

- Headers are safer because URLs get saved in logs and browser history
- GitHub found [more than 39 million leaked secrets](https://github.blog/security/application-security/next-evolution-github-advanced-security/) in 2024
- Committed a key by accident? [Revoke it at once]{.alert} and get a new one. Deleting the file does not help, because Git keeps the history
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 05: pages {#sec:appendix05}
### A loop that asks for one page at a time

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 20px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="56%"}
GDP per capita for every country in 2023, 100 records per page

```python
import time
import requests

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
records = []
page = 1

while True:
    params = {"format": "json", "date": 2023,
              "per_page": 100, "page": page}
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    payload = r.json()

    records.extend(payload[1])
    print("page", page, "of", payload[0]["pages"])

    if page >= payload[0]["pages"]:
        break
    page = page + 1
    time.sleep(0.5)

print(len(records), "records")
```
::::

::::{.column width="44%"}
```text
page 1 of 3
page 2 of 3
page 3 of 3
265 records
```

- `while True:` repeats until a `break`
- The metadata says how many `pages` there are, so the loop knows when to stop
- `records.extend(...)` adds a whole page of records to the list
- `time.sleep(0.5)` waits half a second between requests, to be polite to the server
- A `429` status means you are asking too fast. Wait and try again
- The saved pages are in [`data/`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/tree/main/lectures/lecture-19/data) (`wb_gdppc_2023_page1.json` to `page3`)
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 06: how the course panel was built {#sec:appendix06}
### The script, the columns, and the eight indicator codes

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 20px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
`data/wdi_panel.parquet` holds eight indicators for every country (regional and income groups such as "World" are dropped) from 1990 to 2023, in long format

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `country` | category | Country name |
| `iso3` | category | Three-letter country code |
| `indicator` | category | Short name, one of the eight |
| `year` | int16 | 1990 to 2023 |
| `value` | float64 | The observation, `NaN` where missing |
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
| Short name | WDI code |
|---|---|
| `gdp_per_capita` | `NY.GDP.PCAP.KD` |
| `population` | `SP.POP.TOTL` |
| `life_expectancy` | `SP.DYN.LE00.IN` |
| `co2_per_capita` | `EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5` |
| `internet_users_pct` | `IT.NET.USER.ZS` |
| `urban_pop_pct` | `SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS` |
| `fertility_rate` | `SP.DYN.TFRT.IN` |
| `primary_enrolment_net` | `SE.PRM.NENR` |

The script is [`data/build_wdi_panel.py`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-19/data/build_wdi_panel.py). It saves the raw replies in `data/raw/`, so a second run makes no network requests
